paragraphs.heading: What the hypothesis says
paragraphs.text: The Vine–Matthews–Morley hypothesis says that Earth's oceanic crust acts as a recorder. As seafloor spreading goes on, the crust records reversals in the direction of the geomagnetic field. The hypothesis ties the symmetric magnetic patterns seen on the seafloor to those reversals. It was the first key scientific test of seafloor spreading. Its key impact was that it let the rates of plate motion at mid-ocean ridges be computed.

paragraphs.heading: Who thought of it
paragraphs.text: Harry Hess put forward the seafloor spreading hypothesis in 1960 and published it in 1962. In his account, convection of the Earth's mantle created seafloor at mid-oceanic ridges and pushed the older crust away from the ridge, spreading it. Frederick John Vine, a geophysicist, and Lawrence Morley, a Canadian geologist, independently realized what should follow if Hess was right. Symmetric patterns of magnetization reversals should appear in the rocks surrounding the mid-oceanic ridges. Morley sent letters to Nature in February 1963 and to the Journal of Geophysical Research in April 1963, and both were rejected. That left Vine to publish the theory first, in September 1963, together with Drummond Hoyle Matthews, his PhD adviser at Cambridge University.

paragraphs.heading: Doubt, then support
paragraphs.text: Some colleagues were skeptical. The hypothesis made numerous assumptions: seafloor spreading, geomagnetic reversals and remanent magnetism, all of them hypotheses that were still not widely accepted. Further evidence came in 1964, when Allan V. Cox and colleagues measured the remanent magnetization of lavas from sites on land. Heirtzler added more with a magnetic anomaly profile from the Pacific-Antarctic Ridge that was remarkably symmetric.

paragraphs.heading: How the crust keeps a record
paragraphs.text: At a mid-ocean ridge, new crust is made as magma is injected, extruded and solidified. Ferromagnetism becomes possible once that magma cools through the Curie point, and magnetic minerals in the new crust then take on a magnetization direction parallel to the geomagnetic field of that moment. When the crust has fully cooled, those directions are locked in and it is permanently magnetized. Creation of lithosphere at the ridge is considered continuous and symmetrical, and the old crust moves sideways equally on either side. So as geomagnetic reversals happen, the crust on each side of the ridge holds a record of them. Some of it is magnetized in the normal direction, parallel to the current geomagnetic field, and some in the reversed direction, antiparallel to it.

paragraphs.heading: Reading the record
paragraphs.text: A magnetometer towed above the seafloor can read this record, whether it is near the bottom, at the sea surface or airborne. Typically it finds positive, or high, magnetic anomalies over normally magnetized crust and negative, or low, anomalies over reversed crust. The ridge crest has been compared to a twin-headed tape recorder that records the Earth's magnetic history.

paragraphs.heading: What it made possible
paragraphs.text: The hypothesis links seafloor spreading and geomagnetic reversals, and each has expanded knowledge of the other. Early on, only a short record of reversals was available for studies of rocks on land. That was enough to work out how fast many mid-ocean ridges had spread over the last 700,000 years. The method was to locate the reversed crust boundary closest to the ridge crest. Later, marine magnetic anomalies were found to span the vast flanks of the ridges, and drillcores into the crust on those flanks allowed the anomalies to be dated. With time, land and marine data were combined into an accurate geomagnetic reversal time scale covering almost 200 million years.
